procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of conviction passed by the trial Court for the offences under ss. 34, 302 and 506(11) of the Penal Code, 1860
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court set aside the order of conviction imposed by the trial Court and acquitted all three accused of all charges in Criminal Appeal No. 619 of 1997.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The wife of the deceased/complainant, being unsatisfied with the High Court's order of acquittal, appealed to the Supreme Court impugning the judgment passed by the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was right in disbelieving the prosecution story and acquitting the accused/ respondents to avoid grave miscarriage of justice.

facts: The case arose from a land dispute between closely related parties, which resulted in the death of the appellant's husband.
The trial court initially convicted the accused.
However, the High Court overturned this decision, disbelieved the prosecution's story, and acquitted all the accused.
The wife of the deceased then appealed the acquittal to the Supreme Court.
law: The fundamental principle of criminal law applied is that the prosecution has a duty to prove the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.

When the defense alleges that the prosecution has suppressed the true events and created a false narrative with tampered documents, it is the court's duty to scrutinize whether the prosecution has presented a true version of events.
application: The Supreme Court conducted its own "dispassionate judicial scrutiny" of the case and found the prosecution's story to be untrustworthy.
The Court determined that the evidence presented was "full of contradictions" and created "huge suspicion," making it unsafe to convict the accused.
A significant part of the Court's reasoning was a strong criticism of the investigating agency. The Court found that the agency had failed in its duty to bring home the guilt with probable evidence.

Instead, the Court concluded that the investigating agency appeared to have spent its time creating a false narrative of "two occurrences" and substantiating it with tampered evidence, such as by deliberately altering the time in the FIR.
This manipulation by the investigators undermined the credibility of the entire prosecution case.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was correct to disbelieve the prosecution's story and acquit the accused. It found that the High Court had compelling and substantial reasons for its decision, as the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt due to an untrustworthy story, contradictory evidence, and a flawed investigation. Therefore, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was right in disbelieving the prosecution story and acquitting the accused/ respondents to avoid grave miscarriage of justice.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's judgment is perverse and unsustainable as it failed to consider the unimpeachable evidence of an independent eyewitness.
The High Court ignored overwhelming evidence that established the prosecution's case, including the place of occurrence, recovery of weapons, and forensic reports on blood stains.
The view taken by the High Court in acquitting the accused is unsustainable in law.
The prosecution had clearly explained the injuries on a defense witness (DW2), and this was supported by other evidence.
respondent_arguments: The police conducted a tainted investigation to help the appellant and implicate the accused due to their long-strained relationship.
The deceased was the one who initiated violence and badly injured a defense witness (DW2).
The police created evidence to prevent the accused from taking a plea of self-defense.
The police conducted an illegitimate enquiry, such as recording the statement of a severely injured witness (DW2) without a doctor's certificate.
A key piece of prosecution evidence (Ext. P 14) was a creation of the investigating agency to magnify the case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is not safe to fasten liability on an accused when the evidence is full of contradictions and creates suspicion, as the prosecution has a duty to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.
obiter: The investigating agency ignored its paramount duty of bringing home the guilt of the accused with probable evidence as admissible under law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Applying dispassionate judicial scrutiny, the court found the prosecution's story was not trustworthy to prove the guilt of the accused. The material on record created huge suspicion, and the evidence was so full of contradictions that it was not safe to fasten liability on the accused.
legal_tests_applied: The prosecution has a duty of proving the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
why_appellant_lost: The prosecution story was not trustworthy and the evidence adduced on record was full of contradictions.
The court found force in the respondent's contention that a key piece of evidence, Ext. P 14, was an "oblivious and unduly creation of investigating agency to magnify the case of prosecution."
The prosecution failed to exonerate itself from the duty of proving the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
why_respondent_won: The High Court had compelling and substantial reasons to set aside the conviction and sentence awarded by the trial Court.
The material on record portrayed huge suspicion in the court's mind, making it unsafe to fasten liability on the accused.
The investigating agency appeared to have spent time and mind on creating two occurrences and substantiating them with circumstances, rather than conducting a proper investigation.
policy_considerations: The investigating agency ignored its paramount duty of bringing home the guilt of the accused with probable evidence as admissible under law.
It is not safe to fasten liability on an accused based on evidence that is full of contradictions and creates huge suspicion.
